# SBM-2 – INTERESTS AND VIEWS OF STAKEHOLDERS

The materiality assessment makes it possible to identify the environmental, social and governance topics relating to the most significant IRGs for Juventus. In this process, openness, dialogue and interaction with its internal and external stakeholders are essential requirements in order to understand their needs, interests and expectations, and also to identify the best ways to generate shared value in the medium and long term.

During the season, the Club decided to optimise its stakeholder engagement process with the aim of strengthening listening and, consequently, refining the materiality analysis. A mapping of the stakeholder categories with which the Company interacts and the existing dialogue channels was carried out. Subsequently, stakeholders were prioritised with the aim of defining the objectives and methods of involvement. These elements contributed to the drafting of the stakeholder engagement plan.

In particular,

JUVENTUS ADOPTED A STRUCTURED APPROACH TO STAKEHOLDER ENGAGEMENT WITH REFERENCE TO THE STANDARD AA1000 STAKEHOLDER ENGAGEMENT STANDARD (AA1000), RECOGNISED INTERNATIONALLY AS A METHODOLOGICAL FRAMEWORK FOR MANAGING ENGAGEMENT PROCESSES.

The AA1000 Standard provides operational guidelines for developing effective and transparent engagement processes based on three main phases:

- Identification of material stakeholders;
- Analysis and prioritisation;
- Definition of the most appropriate involvement methods depending on materiality and context.

Consistent with this methodological framework, Juventus has adopted its own integrated approach, combining the Standard's indications with contributions from academic literature. In particular, the prioritisation of stakeholders was conducted by applying the Salience Model developed by Mitchell, Agle and Wood (1997), which allows the degree of materiality of stakeholders to be assessed on the basis of three distinctive attributes:

- Power, i.e. the ability of the stakeholder to influence the Company's activities;
- Legitimacy, understood as the organisation's responsibility to the stakeholder;
- Urgency, which represents the level of critical issues or timeliness of the existing relationship.

Based on the evidence that emerged from this analysis, the Club then identified the most effective methods of involvement for each stakeholder category, in line with the principles of the Standard AA1000. This enabled an open and targeted dialogue to be activated, aimed at listening and understanding the expectations expressed by stakeholders regarding the

Club's strategy and activities. In fact, a first level of involvement was established, distinguishing between direct and indirect methods: the first involved direct interaction with stakeholders through the tool considered the most appropriate, while the second involved a meeting with the company function that manages relations with the reference category.

The first tool used was the interviews with management, conducted with the IRO Owners that made it possible to integrate the internal perspective into the overall assessment of IROs by area of competence.

Another tool used was questionnaires through the materiality analysis with the aim of understanding the importance attributed to the Company's ESG issues by some stakeholder categories.

In addition, a workshop was promoted dedicated to exploring sustainability topics in greater depth, with the aim of fostering direct dialogue between the Company and its strategic stakeholders.

The workshop was used to ask the majority shareholder (Exor) to assess IROs in order to obtain a greater understanding of perspectives and expectations with a view to sustainable development. The meeting generated significant insights into the Company's priorities for action.

## IMPACT, RISK AND OPPORTUNITY MANAGEMENT

### IRO-1 – DESCRIPTION OF THE PROCESS TO IDENTIFY AND ASSESS MATERIAL IMPACTS, RISKS AND OPPORTUNITIES

The materiality analysis is the process that Juventus uses annually to focus, identify and prioritise the most material sustainability matters for itself and its stakeholders on the economy, environment and people, including human rights.

DURING THE 2024/2025 SEASON, IN COMPLIANCE WITH THE REQUIREMENTS OF THE NEW EUROPEAN DIRECTIVE 2022/24EA (CORPORATE SUSTAINABILITY REPORTING DIRECTIVE), THE CLUB STARTED THE DOUBLE MATERIALITY ASSESSMENT PROCESS, FOLLOWING THE PROVISIONS OF THE (EU) DELEGATED REGULATION

98

Annual Report as at 30 June 2025

99

Juventus Football Club S.p.A.

--- pág. 51 ---

JUVENTUS

# 2023/2772 OF THE EUROPEAN COMMISSION - WHICH INTRODUCED THE EUROPEAN SUSTAINABILITY REPORTING STANDARDS ("ESRS") - AND THE IMPLEMENTATION GUIDANCE "EFRAQ 161 MATERIALITY ASSESSMENT".

According to these methodologies, a topic is material if it is important from the point of view of impact materiality (inside- out perspective), financial materiality (outside-in perspective) or from both perspectives.

In particular, the inside-out impact perspective or logic assesses the materiality of the impacts in terms of impacts on the economy, the environment and people, including those on human rights, related to business operations and the upstream and downstream value chain. This approach makes it possible to assess how the Company affects the external context, identifying the areas where it is possible to further improve to amplify positive impacts, or where it is necessary to intervene to mitigate and prevent any negative impacts.

On the other hand, the outside-in financial perspective or logic assesses the sustainability aspects that generate risks or opportunities that have or which can reasonably be expected to have a material influence on the undertaking's development, its financial position, economic result, cash flows, access to finance or short-, medium- or long-term cost of capital. The Club materiality analysis process was broken down into three main phases:

- Understanding of the internal and external context;
- Identification of the IROs related to sustainability matters;
- Assessment and identification of material IROs.

## UNDERSTANDING OF THE INTERNAL AND EXTERNAL CONTEXT

The process initiated to identify significant IROs for Juventus began with an in-depth analysis of the internal and external context. This analysis took into account the best practices of the sector, market dynamics and the company's specific business model.

To conduct these analyses, a benchmark analysis was also carried out for a panel of industry companies (national and international clubs). The various company departments were consulted to identify risks and opportunities.

## IDENTIFICATION OF IROS RELATED TO SUSTAINABILITY MATTERSUE

The mapping of impacts (impact materiality) was carried out after understanding the internal and external context of the Company, taking into account the Topics and Sub-Topics defined by the ESRS. To identify risks and opportunities (financial materiality), particular attention was paid to their relationship with the positive and negative impacts already mapped in the context of impact materiality, as well as any dependencies. In addition, to identify risks and opportunities, the relevant available documentation available within the ERM was analysed in order to create an alignment with the company risk assessment and management methodology.

○ STATUTORY FINANCIAL STATEMENTS

This process resulted in a first photograph, in which the impacts were classified as positive or negative, current or potential, also identifying the phase of the value chain in which they stand (upstream processes, business activities, downstream processes).

## ASSESSMENT AND IDENTIFICATION OF MATERIAL IROS - IMPACT MATERIALITY

The impact materiality assessment took place with the involvement of the main company functions. In particular, one-to-one meetings were organised with: Facilities Management, People, Culture & ESG, Team Manager, Procurement, Stadium & Consumer Business, Marketing, Legal, Risk & Compliance and Partnership.

The significance of an impact was determined on the basis of its severity, and the likelihood of occurrence. The severity of an impact was established by assessing:

- Scale: how serious the negative impact is or how many benefits the positive impact on people or the environment entails;
- Scope: how widespread the impacts are (e.g., how geographically extensive an environmental damage is), or how many people are affected by company activities;

In addition, with regard to negative impacts only, the fol-

lowing were assessed:

- Irremediable character: if and to what extent it is possible to remediate negative impacts, i.e. by bringing the environment or people concerned back to their original state;
- Impact on human rights.

## ASSESSMENT AND IDENTIFICATION OF MATERIAL IROS - FINANCIAL MATERIALITY

The financial materiality assessment took place through the assessment of the significance of risks and opportunities considering financial metrics and reputational metrics. Specifically, the determination of significance is based on a combination of probability and impact of financial effects in the short (within 1 year), medium (1 to 3 years) and long (more than 3 years) term. The impact of the financial effects was defined using the ERM methodology and the probability defined on a 5-level scale. It should be noted that, if it was not possible to quantify the economic and financial effects of a risk or opportunity, in accordance with the provisions of the EFRAG Guidelines, a qualitative metric was applied in order to measure the reputational impact, which may compromise the relationship with the Group's main stakeholders in terms of funds and cost of capital and therefore be financially material.

# ASSESSMENT AND IDENTIFICATION OF MATERIAL IROS – RESULTS

Following the IRO-related assessments, two materiality thresholds (one for impact materiality and one for financial materiality) were established, beyond which these elements were considered material. These thresholds are an essential criterion for identifying issues that can significantly influence the decisions of investors and all other stakeholders of Juventus.

A double materiality matrix, a graphic representation of the material topics and their positioning in relation to the level of relevance was subsequently developed.

# MDR-P – POLICIES, ACTIONS, MDR-P METRICS AND TARGETS MDR-P

In the following sections of this document, Juventus has disclosed the policies and actions adopted to manage the IRDs related to material sustainability matters, in compliance with the requirements of the relevant ESRS topics. Actions, metrics and targets were identified in line with the targets of the ESG strategy, in fact, the Club chose to direct its efforts on certain topics. The issues currently not covered will be addressed in the coming years through targeted actions, with the aim of promptly and gradually responding to all identified needs. Where available, metrics and targets have been integrated into the disclosure, ensuring consi-

consistency with the actions described and providing a clear picture of the Company's performance and progress.

Juventus does not currently have a structured process to communicate the amount of current economic and financial resources compared to the most relevant amounts presented in the financial statements. However, where possible, the Club undertakes to give an overview of the expenses and investments made for the implementation of the activities expressed in the respective sections.

# TAXONOMY

# THE EUROPEAN TAXONOMY

This chapter contains information in accordance with the provisions of Art. Article 8 of European Union (EU) Taxonomy Regulation 2020/852. This information is provided in accordance with the criteria established by other delegated acts issued by the European Commission and available as at the date of publication of the Consolidated Sustainability Statement, in particular:

- Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2139 of 4 June 2021 (Delegated Act on the Climate);
- Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2178 of 6 July 2021 (Delegated Act on Disclosure);
- Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/1214 of 9 March 2022 (Complementary Delegated Act on the Climate);
- Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2485 of 27 June 2023 amending the Delegated Act on the Climate;
- Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2486 of 27 June 2023 (Environmental Delegated Act).

# REGULATORY CONTEXT

In accordance with EU Regulation 2020/852 (hereinafter referred to as the "Taxonomy Regulation"), the European Taxonomy ("Taxonomy") is a fundamental tool introduced as part of the European Green Deal, with the target of achieving the environmental and climate targets set out in the pact, in particular decarbonisation by 2050. The Taxonomy Regulation provides detailed guidelines on the economic activities considered environmentally sustainable, with the aim of increasing transparency for investors and contrasting greenwashing. It also supports companies in the energy transition process and in the adoption of more sustainable environmental policies.

The Taxonomy constitutes a fundamental cornerstone of the Sustainable Finance Action Plan, with the aim of guiding capital flows towards a more environmentally responsible economy. It is a decisive step towards achieving carbon neutrality by 2050, by means of de-

fining criteria for identifying environmentally sustainable economic activities.

The European Taxonomy includes six environmental targets:

- Climate change mitigation.
- Climate change adaptation.
- Sustainable use and protection of water and marine resources.
- Transition to a circular economy.
- Pollution prevention and control.
- Protection and restoration of biodiversity and ecosystems.

The Taxonomy Regulation stipulates that an activity can be considered aligned with one or more environmental targets if all of the following criteria are met:

- It substantially contributes to one or more environmental targets.
- It does not cause significant harm to any of the environmental targets (principle of the Do No Significant Harm - DNSH).
- It is carried out in compliance with the minimum safeguarding criteria.
- It observes the technical screening criteria.

To ensure compliance with the indications contained in the Delegated Acts relating to the six environmental objectives, a three-step process was developed:

1. The first phase envisaged a preliminary analysis of the sectors falling within the six environmental targets, identifying certain economic activities falling within the following targets as potentially eligible for Juventus' business: climate change mitigation; climate change adaptation; transition to a circular economy; protection and restoration of biodiversity and ecosystems.
2. Subsequently, the screening phase was launched with the aim of identifying the eligible economic activities for each environmental target. Through

the direct involvement of units, the economic activities that generated Turnover, CapEx and/or OpEx during the reporting period were then mapped. In the case of economic activities applicable to several environmental targets, in view of Juventus' business and strategy, it was decided to prioritise the Climate change mitigation target. The eligible economic activities fall under the following environmental targets: climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation; protection and restoration of biodiversity and ecosystems.

3. The verification of the alignment was then carried out by Juventus in compliance with the provisions of the Regulation, mapping:

- the substantial contribution to achieving one or more environmental objectives;
- compliance with the DNSH principle;
- observance of minimum safeguarding criteria;
- compliance with the technical screening criteria.
It should be noted that, since Juventus has not performed an analysis of exposure to the risk of climate change with the aim of developing targeted adaptation strategies (as required by the Regulation, ref. Climate Change Adaptation), screening activities were concluded during the verification of compliance with the DNSH principle and it was not deemed necessary to verify compliance with the minimum safeguarding criteria.

4. As a last step, the economic indicators required by the Regulation were calculated. For further information, please refer to the section "Reporting results and criteria".

### ELIGIBILITY ANALYSIS

An economic activity is considered eligible according to the European Taxonomy if it is explicitly included in the Taxonomy Regulation due to its substantial contribution to achieving one or more environmental targets, regardless of whether or not that activity meets the technical screening criteria set out therein.

#### CapEx

This refers to the proportion of economic activities eligible under the Taxonomy in terms of capital expenditure, defined as investments eligible under the Taxonomy (numerator) divided by total investments (denominator).

Within the capital expenditure considered eligible, the following were included:

- The investment for the rental fee of cars included in the company car fleet of Juventus and of J Hotel;
- The maintenance work for the revamping of the internal areas of Vinovo's Next Gen locker room.
- The assets owned by the company (Allianz Stadium, JTCV, Juventus Headquarters ("JHQ"), JTCC).

Below is a summary of the identified activities and their correspondence with the economic activities of the European Taxonomy Regulation.

#### OpEx

This refers to the proportion of economic activities eligible under the Taxonomy in terms of operating costs, defined as eligible costs (numerator) divided by total costs (denominator). The total OpEx includes non-capitalised direct costs related to research and development, building renovation measures, short-term leases and all forms of maintenance and repair.

To determine which of Juventus' activities can be linked to those identified by the European Taxonomy, the main business activities were mapped and analysed.

No activities were identified within operating expenditure considered eligible.

#### TURNOVER

This refers to the proportion of economic activities eligible under the Taxonomy in terms of turnover, defined as part of net revenues associated with economic activities aligned with the Taxonomy (numerator) divided by net revenues (denominator).

Below is a summary of the identified activities and their correspondence with the economic activities of the European Taxonomy Regulation.

### ALIGNMENT ANALYSIS

In order to be considered aligned with the Taxonomy, an economic activity must contribute substantially to one or more environmental objectives, while not causing significant harm to other environmental objectives.

Therefore, after verifying compliance with the substantial contribution criteria required for each of the above economic activities, Juventus proceeded to verify compliance with DNSH principles and, specifically, in relation to DNSH on Climate Adaptation (which requires compliance with Appendix A), the Club reports that, although it does not currently have an assessment of the exposure to climate risk factors of its activities and assets (an assessment to be carried out through an analysis of the acute and chronic risks to which the activities are subject), it has begun to lay the groundwork to be able to carry out such activities.

For the reasons mentioned above, the alignment analysis is therefore currently not compliant with the requirements of the Regulation.

# ENVIRONMENTAL INFORMATION

The protection of the planet is a strategic ESG priority for Juventus, not only as a football club, but also as a business with an impact and visibility worldwide. In a context in which environmental challenges – from climate change to water management, to the transition to circular models – are becoming increasingly important, organisations must play an active role in promoting sustainable and responsible practices. Confirming this commitment, Juventus has dedicated two of the six pillars of its ESG Strategy to environmental aspects, consistent with the requirements of the ESRS 2 – Strategy, business model and materiality (SBM-1

- Strategy, business model and value chain) standard. This choice demonstrates the Company's desire to consolidate and expand a virtuous path of sustainable environmental management, already started in previous years and strengthened today through the definition of progressive targets, the implementation of targeted actions and the transparent monitoring of results.

This path is also developed through participation in national and international networks dedicated to the environmental topic.

# THE CLUB IS ALSO ACTIVELY INVOLVED IN THE EUROPEAN STADIUM & SAFETY MANAGEMENT ASSOCIATION ("ESSMA"), IN WHICH IT HOLDS A LEADERSHIP ROLE:

Since 2018, Francesco Gianello, Facilities Management Director of the Club, is a member of the Advisory Committee and, since 2025, its Chair. In this context, Juventus participates in working tables on environmental sustainability, as in June 2025 at the Johan Cruijff Arena in Amsterdam, presenting the Road to Al-

lianz Stadium sustainable mobility project.

At the football system level, Juventus participates in the sustainability committees of Lega Serie A, contributing to the definition and implementation of the "CSR – Calcio Social Responsibility 2030" strategy. The Club also collaborates with UEFA, with which it is aligned with the sustainability strategy Strength Through Unity 2030, participating in dedicated workshops and training programmes. These include participation in the international "Sustainability in Football Compact Course", promoted by UEFA Academy and ECA with the academic support of SDA Bocconi. Finally, Juventus is also aligned with the sustainability strategy of FIGC and ECA thus strengthening its commitment to this topic at national and European level.

# E1 CLIMATE CHANGE

Juventus is committed to monitoring and reporting annually on its energy consumption and Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions and, from the 2024/2025 season, also Scope 3 emissions, with the aim of reducing its environmental impact and identifying opportunities for improvement in terms of efficiency.

To this end, again this year the Club made use of the advice of the Sant'Anna School of Advanced Studies in Pisa, a well-established collaboration, expanded with an integrated approach of Life Cycle Assessment ("LCA") and Carbon Footprint aligned with the CSRD directives.

# GOV-3 – INTEGRATION OF SUSTAINABILITY-RELATED PERFORMANCE IN INCENTIVE SCHEMES

The Juventus Remuneration Policy is detailed within the chapter "General Disclosures" in section ESRS 2 GOV-3 – "Integration of sustainability-related performance in incentive schemes". You can also consult it in full at the following link on the Juventus website, Remuneration and equity investments | Juventus Club, with reference to the 2024/25 season.

Specifically with regard to the STI Plan, this is structured with a single scorecard, consisting of three macro-targets: an economic and financial KPI, strategic KPIs for each function and an ESG KPI, as an individual target relating to environmental sustainability parameters, promotion of a sustainable culture and reduction of operating costs. # E1-1 – TRANSITION PLAN FOR CLIMATE
CHANGE MITIGATION

Juventus contributes to climate change mitigation through
its ESG strategy "Black, White & More". The pillar dedicated
to this area, called "Emissions in the Corner", aims
to achieve emission reduction targets through different
actions illustrated in section E1-3 – "Actions and resources
in relation to climate change policies", related to the
following areas:

- the self-generation of renewable energy;
- improving energy efficiency;
- the promotion of sustainable mobility practices
among fans.

These measures represent a concrete contribution to
emission reduction.

The Club also recognises the importance of having a
structured climate transition plan pursuant to ESRS E1
with quantitative objectives and time-bound targets, and
is committed to developing it in the coming years, in line
with regulatory requirements and European standards.
This step will, in any case, only represent the final step
along a solid environmental path, which has long been
started. In recent years, Juventus has progressively integrated
its environmental actions within a strategic framework, and
more specifically, into the two environmental pillars of
the Black, White and More ESG strategy: Emissions in the
Corner and Assist to Circularity. These initiatives, illustrated
in the following sections, develop in consistency and
harmony with the Club's certified en-

vironmental management systems (ISO 14001 and ISO
20121), which in any case provide for the annual definition
of targets and actions of continuous improvement.

The next step will therefore be to structure a climate transition
plan that, in line with the two environmental pillars of the
strategy and with the targets of the certified management
systems, is fully aligned with the requirements of ESRS E1.

The double materiality assessment carried out by Juventus, whose methodological approach is described in the section "General Disclosures", identified the IROs related to the topic of climate change. The IROs related to this topic are closely related to Juventus' strategy and business model, with particular reference to GHG emissions generated, energy efficiency, and the physical risk to which assets and infrastructures are exposed.

Specifically, the three negative impacts resulting from the materiality assessment are related to the genera-

tion of GHG emissions. To address and mitigate these impacts, Juventus monitors Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions and pursues specific actions. The three positive impacts and opportunity are related to energy consumption and asset efficiency. The only risk related to climate change adaptation refers to extreme climate events (acute physical risk) with possible damage to infrastructure and interruptions in sports activities with a consequent impact on costs and revenues.

### IRO-1 – DESCRIPTION OF THE PROCESSES TO IDENTIFY AND ASSESS MATERIAL CLIMATE-RELATED IMPACTS, RISKS AND OPPORTUNITIES

The process for identifying and assessing material IROs related to climate change is described in the chapter "General disclosures" within the section on the double materiality assessment process.

To ensure that the carbon footprint assessment is as accurate and transparent as possible, the Company thoroughly examines its GHG emissions inventory, which is continuously improved and updated to include all climate-changing emissions and related sources.

These emissions are divided into three categories:

- Scope 1, i.e. direct emissions from sources owned or controlled by the organisation, such as the combustion of fossil material;
- Scope 2, i.e. indirect emissions from electricity purchased and used by the organisation;
- Scope 3, i.e. other indirect emissions generated along the organisation's value chain, which include activities such as staff commuting, fans' travelling for Club matches and the production of purchased goods and services.

Juventus monitors all the above categories, where Scope 3 emissions represent the largest share of the overall report.

### E1-2 POLICIES RELATED TO CLIMATE CHANGE MITIGATION AND ADAPTATION

The Black, White & More strategy represents the continuation of a structured environmental management path, which in recent years has allowed the Club to achieve important awards on the topic of sustainability.

• IN 2019, ALLIANZ STADIUM ACHIEVED THE ISO 14001 CERTIFICATION, AN INTERNATIONAL STANDARD THAT DEFINES THE REQUIREMENTS FOR AN ENVIRONMENTAL MANAGEMENT SYSTEM AIMED AT MONITORING AND REDUCING THE DIRECT AND INDIRECT ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACTS OF ACTIVITIES. THIS CERTIFICATION WAS SUBSEQUENTLY EXTENDED ALSO TO THE JUVENTUS TRAINING CENTER - CONTINASSA ("JTCC") IN 2022, STRENGTHENING THE CLUB'S SYSTEMIC APPROACH TO MANAGING ENVIRONMENTAL PERFORMANCE.

# CODE OF ETHICS

The environmental policies are based on the Code of Ethics ("Code of Ethics") (see the section "Governance Information") which establishes the principles relating to environmental sustainability.

In particular, aware of the priority need to create value and maintain a relationship of trust with its stakeholders, Juventus recognises the importance of integrating sustainability into its business model, actively engaging in:

- periodic reporting on its environmental impact in the sustainability reporting;
- continuous contribution of improvements to environmental protection, minimising the environmental impact from the performance of its social activities and the operation, construction and maintenance of the sites and facilities it owns;

- adoption of responsible approaches towards the protection of the environment, acting in strict compliance with applicable regulations.

It is possible to consult the Code of Ethics in full at the following link Corporate Governance | Juventus Club.

# ENVIRONMENTAL POLICY

As part of its activities, Juventus pursues the target of reducing environmental impact through the adoption of an Environmental Policy compliant with the requirements of the UNI EN ISO 14001:2015 Standard. This choice represents a concrete commitment not only to those who have an employment relationship with the Company, but also to all those who use its sports entertainment services.

Among the key principles of the Policy, whose internal contact person is the Juventus Environmental Delegate, are the promotion of an environmental sustainability culture, aimed at systematically reducing impacts, and the adoption of a process of constant analysis and monitoring of activities to implement prevention and continuous improvement measures. Juventus is also committed to ensuring that its processes are adapted to sustainability needs and to appoint a dedicated manager for the coordination of environmental actions.

The Policy also defines specific operational targets, including:

- preventing and minimising environmental risks and impacts related to sports and entertainment activities;
- ensure responsible behaviour by Juventus staff both during their work and in their daily lives, in line with national awareness campaigns;
- maintaining a structured training course for all staff, aimed at strengthening skills and awareness on environmental topics;
- engaging customers and suppliers, promoting "environmental" evaluation criteria in product and service choices and promoting collaborations with institutions, civil society organisations and the world of research.

The Juventus Environment Policy is available in full at the following link Policies and Procedures | Juventus Club.

# POLICY FOR SUSTAINABLE EVENT MANAGEMENT

Juventus has adopted a Sustainable Event Management Policy with the target of integrating sustainability principles into its business activities, recognising the strong social and environmental impact that sport can generate.

# IN THIS CONTEXT, A CLUB WITH THE JUVENTUS' INTERNATIONAL RESONANCE PLAYS AN IMPORTANT ROLE IN HELPING TO REDEFINE BUSINESS MODELS IN A SUSTAINABLE KEY AND IN DRIVING CHANGE IN THE SECTOR.

Juventus recognises its responsibility both as a sports company and as a football company, and therefore has decided to actively contribute to the achievement of some SDGs, including: Good Health and Well-Being (SDG 3), Quality Education (SDG 4), Reduced Inequalities (SDG 10), Climate Action (SDG 13).

The Policy, whose internal contact person is the Sustainable Event Management System Officer, finds its concrete application especially in the organisation of the match day event, which represents much more than 90 minutes of play: it is a show that involves fans and enthusiasts through entertainment fan activities, choreographies and sharing opportunities. The guiding principle is that the event is sustainable, inclusive, safe and entertaining. For this reason, Juventus has adopted a Management System for the Sustainability of Events, in compliance with the UNI ISO 20121 standard - the international standard that defines the requirements for the planning and sustainable management of events - establishing, documenting and implementing dedicated procedures, with the commitment to improve continuity and effectiveness over time.

# E1-3 – ACTIONS AND RESOURCES IN RELATION TO CLIMATE CHANGE POLICIES

To counteract the impacts resulting from GHG emissions generated by its sport and business activities and along its value chain, Juventus adopts measures to reduce its emissions, improve energy efficiency, promote supply from renewable sources and raise the awareness of its stakeholders about the importance of environmental protection.

During the 2024/2025 season,

THE CLUB IMPLEMENTED A SERIES OF INITIATIVES AIMED AT CONTRIBUTING TO CLIMATE CHANGE MITIGATION, IN COMPLIANCE WITH THE TARGETS OF THE "EMISSIONS IN THE CORNER" PILLAR OF THE BLACK, WHITE & MORE ESG STRATEGY

(see ESRS 2 in the section SBM-1 – "Strategy, business model and value chain").

The main actions taken are illustrated in detail below.

# RENEWABLE ENERGY

In order to minimise the environmental impact of electricity consumption, since the 2018/2019 season the Club has been sourcing its electricity exclusively from renewable sources* through specific agreements with suppliers.

Therefore, all Juventus sites use 100% electricity from renewable sources. This is a conscious choice, which involves significant investment but which has been adopted to ensure consistency with the Club's environmental commitments.

Procurement is certified through Guarantees of Origin ("GO"), issued in compliance with European regulations, which transparently certify the renewable origin of purchased energy. In this way, the entire Club's electricity demand is covered by certified sources, contributing to indirect electricity-related emission reduction (Scope 2).

On the energy self-generation front, Juventus has made some initial steps, through small plants that represent a first approach to this supply mode. Currently self-production is mainly limited to the photovoltaic plant installed at the JTC; although not directly owned by the Club, Juventus manages its production and related administration (compilation of registers and transmission of data to the Customs Agency).

In addition to this, two solar thermal plants are present within the Allianz Stadium, active but with a minimal and limited contribution to the production of sanitary hot water. The stadium is also equipped with a photovoltaic system on its roof, built in the past but not operational, due to the small size and complexity of the authorisation process with respect to the expected benefits.

Finally, feasibility studies were carried out over the years to assess further self-generation opportunities – particularly a project concerning the stadium, headquarters and training center – whose outcomes remain at the assessment stage.

# ENERGY EFFICIENCY

The Facility & Maintenance Team is constantly monitoring and optimising energy consumption, through targeted control, plant efficiency and technological updating interventions. The Club has employed a UNI CEI 11339-certified Energy Manager as EGE (Expert in Energy Management) and appointed at FIRE (Italian Federation for the Rational Use of Energy), in accordance with Italian Law 10/91, which supports the development of energy projects, including energy diagnosis and the implementation of an Energy Management pathway.

The actions to support the energy efficiency path are shown below:

# Management and monitoring systems:

- since its opening (2011), the Allianz Stadium has been equipped with a Building Management System ("BMS") that allows the automatic planning and regulation of the operation of electrical and thermal fluid systems (on/off, set point, alarms, diagnostics);
- since 2017, this approach has also been extended to the headquarters and the JTCC site, while the Vinovo site remains partially excluded due to its greater plant complexity;
- dedicated metrics were installed to monitor consumption of the various utilities and verify billing accuracy. These data are collected and analysed through a digital monitoring platform developed with the support of the Information & Communication Technology Team, which is also useful for consumption and cost forecasting activities.

# Lighting:

• OVER THE YEARS, MOST OF THE LIGHTING SYSTEMS WERE CONVERTED TO LED LAMPS;

- with regard to the Allianz Stadium, over the years there has been a progressive transition to LED lamps (to date about 85% of the stadium area surfaces are covered by LEDs), which has allowed a reduction in energy consumption and maintenance, replacement and disposal costs. Specifically, the power of the lighting system was reduced by approximately 24% for the pitch. In addition to the environmental benefits, the new LED lighting system has made the pitch and hospitality areas welcoming and spectacular environments. In particular, outstanding results have been achieved in terms of colour rendition, image uniformity, flickering absence and glare reduction, also ensuring visual comfort for the players, the fans in the Stadium and the crowd at home, now able to enjoy television footage that authentically reproduces what is happening on the pitch;

- at Vinovo the lighting systems of three pitches and of the internal premises have already been converted; therefore, the remaining five pitches remain to be completed;
- the headquarters and the JTCC have been equipped with LED lighting for their interior spaces since their inauguration.

# HVAC systems (Heating, Ventilation and Air Conditioning):

- the hospitality areas of the stadium were equipped with inverters to allow for the regulation of air ventilation based on their actual occupation, with benefits on non-match days.

# Structural constraints:

- some significant consumption, such as lamps for the grass growth (equal to about 25-30% of the stadium electric consumption) and pitch heating systems (Stadium and JTC), today represent one of the main energy-intensive factors and, for functional and grass maintenance reasons, are not easily reducible. Precisely for this reason they represent one of the main challenges for the future, when the Club intends to assess innovative and technological solutions capable of reducing their impact;
- the use hours of lighting systems are already optimised to the extent permitted by regulatory and safety requirements.

*With the exception of consumption related to district heating and cooling.

## SUSTAINABLE MOBILITY OF FANS: ROAD TO ALLIANZ STADIUM

Fan mobility is one of the most significant environmental challenges for a sports club. According to a study conducted by the Sant'Anna School of Advanced Studies in Pisa, fans' travel in fact account for between 50% and 70% of the total emissions of a football club, with a particularly significant impact related to the prevailing use of private cars and, in some cases, flights, especially for clubs such as Juventus, which have a large and nationally and internationally distributed fan base.

To address this issue, Juventus has adopted a three-track approach:

Dialogue with fans, with the aim of collecting accurate data on travel habits and understanding their needs, in order to develop effective solutions both from an environmental and fan experience point of view. With this in mind, a fans survey was launched also in the 2024/2025 season, which included the topic of mobility.

Dialogue with football sector stakeholders, as this is a common challenge for all clubs. Participation in working tables, conferences and networks (e.g. Lega Serie A, UEFA) allows to share experiences and good practices. Recent examples include the participation of Juventus at the Event Sustainability table during the UEFA 2025 Respect Forum (7–8 May, Zurich) and the presentation of a case study at the ESSMA Meeting (16–17 June, Amsterdam).

Dialogue with local authorities: interactions with the Municipality of Turin and the Turin public transport company (GTT) were crucial to the development of projects on the topic.

To celebrate Earth Day (22 April 2025), Juventus launched a sustainable mobility pilot project for home matches, carried out in collaboration with GTT and with the support of Allianz. In particular, for the Juventus–Monza (27 April 2025) and Juventus–Udinese (18 May 2025) matches, fans under 30 received a free daily local public transport ticket, valid for the entire match day and usable without limits on the urban network, including the subway.

## CALLED ROAD TO ALLIANZ STADIUM, THE INITIATIVE WAS A FIRST CONCRETE STEP TO ENCOURAGE PUBLIC TRANSPORT USE AND REDUCE THE ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT OF MATCH-RELATED TRAVEL.

Launched in the urban area, the project intends to be progressively extended in the next seasons and is part of the Black, White & More Club ESG strategy, in particular in relation to the “Emissions in the Corner” pillar.

As a result of testing on 27 April 2025, the Sant'Anna School of Advanced Studies in Pisa estimated that CO₂ emissions equivalent to those absorbed in a year by 436 trees were prevented, with similar results also recorded during the match against Udinese. This is a positive figure, which confirms the validity of the initiative and demonstrates how Juventus has embarked on a concrete path to tackle the challenge of fan mobility.

¹Estimate carried out considering a baseline defined with a fan mobility questionnaire survey carried out in 2025. Calculations made according to the LCA methodology with the use of SimalPro software, the Ecoinvent 3.10 database, DEFRA 2024 data and national emission factors processed by ISPRA. Source tree absorption data. Life EFFIGE project according to which a tree absorbs an average of 7.5 kg of CO₂ per year.

## INTERNAL SUSTAINABLE MOBILITY

In line with Italian Decree-Law No. 34 of 19 May 2020 (known as the “Recovery Decree”, then converted into Italian Law No. 77 of 17 July 2020), which includes “Measures to incentivise sustainable mobility”, a survey was carried out during the 2021/2022 season to define the Juventus’ Commuting Plan.

The same survey was repeated in the 2023/2024 season. In particular, to identify systematic commuting habits, a questionnaire consisting of around 80 questions was administered to the Club employees between 11 and 13 December 2023.

The main findings were:

- employees’ preferred means for travel is their private car, which is currently perceived as the fastest and most comfortable option;
- the most frequent answers to the question about what types of constraints or incentives could make people give up using cars were:

- willingness to change habits if the public transport offer improved;
- safety improvement on bike lanes;
- carpooling incentives.

# COLLABORATION BETWEEN JUVENTUS AND ONE TREE PLANTED: A CONCRETE COMMITMENT TO THE ENVIRONMENT

The collaboration between Juventus and the non-profit One Tree Planted organisation, which is focused on global reforestation projects, began in 2020 with the ambitious target of planting trees for every goal scored by the Club's teams. Initially, 200 trees were planted for each goal.

25,000 trees were planted in the first season (2020/2021). The following season (2021/2022) kept the level high, with 22,800 trees planted. These trees around the world will capture about 14,400 tons of CO₂ in the first 20 years after their planting.

Juventus informed fans about the progress, sharing the results and celebrating each goal not only as a sporting achievement, but also as a significant contribution to the planet's health.

In 2023, the partnership with One Tree Planted evolved in into a three-year project focused on the Turin metropolitan area. The areas in question included:

- Turin (Mirafiori) | Orti Generali;
- Turin | Cascina Falchera;
- Fiano (Turin) | La Mandria Nature Park.

The goal is to restore vital ecological functions, promote ecosystem health and resilience, and mitigate the effects of greenhouse gases through the capture and storage of carbon dioxide.

# EXTREME WEATHER EVENTS

As part of the double materiality assessment, Juventus identified one of the material risks related to extreme climate phenomena. This risk has been traced back to the corporate risk register (ERM), where it is currently included within the broader "catastrophic events" category, which includes not only natural events (earthquakes, fires, atmospheric events), but also factors of different nature (e.g. terrorist events). Given the growing materiality of climate change, the Club recognises the opportunity to map climate risk independently and more accurately in the coming years, in order to strengthen its ability to identify further mitigation and resilience measures.

To date, Juventus manages the risk with a set of actions already operational. First, the Club has taken out "all risk" insurance policies to cover all its sites, which also include damage resulting from extreme weather events, such as hailstones, sudden floods and storms. Even without an explicit reference to climate

change, insurance cover also de facto extends to weather events whose frequency and intensity are increased by climate change.

Additionally, Juventus has put in place specific maintenance and prevention procedures.

Each year, a technical report and a certificate relating to the structural maintenance of plants are prepared, submitted to the Provincial Commission for the Supervision of Public Performance Spaces ("CPV") of the Turin Prefecture Office. Targeted preventive measures are also in place, such as procedures to reduce the risk of water seepage in the event of heavy rainfall.

These actions represent a first response to climate risk and will be further developed and systematised in the Climate Transition Plan, which the Club undertakes to formalise in the coming years (see section E1-3).

# **E1-4 – TARGETS RELATED TO CLIMATE CHANGE MITIGATION AND ADAPTATION**

As part of its *Black, White & More* ESG strategy, Juventus pursues climate change mitigation and adaptation targets through the “Emissions in the Corner” pillar, with a specific focus on energy efficiency and the use of renewable resources. This path forms the basis for the future definition of structured quantitative targets, in line with ESRS E1, with respect to exploiting opportunities related to decarbonisation and to the enhancement of positive impacts linked to energy efficiency and the use of renewable resources.

In addition, Juventus currently has an operational environmental targets system, defined annually in line with its ISO 14001 and ISO 20121 certified management systems. Among other things, these targets include reducing energy consumption, managing and recycling waste and emission reduction related to employee and fan travel. Although these commitments are not formalised as climate targets, they already contribute

today to both emission mitigation and the strengthening of the Club’s resilience to risks arising from climate change.

Therefore, the next step will be the definition of specific mitigation and adaptation targets, fully aligned with the requirements of ESRS E1, which will be processed in compliance with the two environmental pillar of the Black, White & More ESG strategy (Emissions in the Corner and Assists to Circularity), with the priorities identified by the ERM system on climate risks and with the commitments provided for by certified environmental management systems.

During the 2024/2025 season, Juventus' total energy consumption was 30,501.81 MWh.

A relevant element is the fact that more than one third of the energy needs have been met by electricity certified through Guarantees of Origin, from renewable hydroelectric plants. Moreover, as already mentioned in section E1-1 – "Transition plan for climate change mitigation",

100% OF THE ELECTRICITY PURCHASED BY JUVENTUS COMES FROM RENEWABLE SOURCES, CONFIRMING THE DESIRE TO GIVE PREFERENCE TO SOLUTIONS THAT CAN GENERATE A POSITIVE IMPACT.

Electricity consumption of the company B&W Nest are not covered by Guarantee of Origin, therefore, they do not fall under the portion relating to sustainable supply.

The remaining consumption needs were mainly met through district heating and cooling systems, supplemented by diesel and natural gas, technologies that currently ensure continuity and reliability in the Company's operational activities.

Juventus is fully aware of the challenges that the energy transition poses and intends to face them responsibly and with vision. For this reason, the Club is committed to progressively increasing the use of renewable sources, consolidating a sustainable growth path that combines innovation and respect for the environment.

![img-84.jpeg](img-84.jpeg)

### E1-6 – GROSS SCOPE 1, 2, 3 AND TOTAL GHG EMISSIONS

Starting from the 2019/2020 season, with the support of the Sant'Anna School of Advanced Studies in Pisa, Juventus started to disclose its own carbon footprint, as the Club's commitment to manage its CO₂ emissions¹.

Scope 1 emissions, i.e. direct greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from sources owned and controlled by the Company, mainly concerned emissions from natural gas, diesel-powered electric generator, movements of the company car fleet powered by petrol and diesel and hybrid cars. The total of these emissions was 1,412.1 tCO₂eq.

For the calculation of Scope 2 emissions, i.e. indirect greenhouse gas emissions associated with the energy consumption purchased by the Company from the grid, two distinct methodologies have been used for the calculation:

- Location-based method: based on the average emission factors for regional, sub-national or national power generation. These amounted to 4,728 tCO₂eq.
- Market-based method: which is instead based on the CO₂ emissions emitted by the energy suppliers from which the organisation buys electricity through contracts, or on market-related factors. Purchased electricity from renewable sources, with Guarantee of Origin certificates, are assigned an emission

factor of zero for Scope 2 emissions calculated according to the market-based method. Since the 2018/2019 season, 100% of the electricity purchased by Juventus has come from renewable sources; the relative emission value is 0. These amounted to 2,623 tCO₂eq.

### STARTING FROM THE CURRENT SEASON, JUVENTUS HAS STARTED TO CALCULATE AND REPORT ITS SCOPE 3 EMISSIONS. THESE REFER TO INDIRECT GREENHOUSE GAS EMISSIONS GENERATED ALONG THE CLUB'S VALUE CHAIN, BOTH UPSTREAM AND DOWNSTREAM.

As the GHG Protocol identifies 15 different Scope 3 categories, a materiality assessment was performed on these, with the aim of determining which were material and applicable to Juventus.

The assessment concerned the Scope 3 disclosures of four peers, all European football clubs. The parameters considered were: materiality for the Company, transparency on the calculation methodology, accessibility, accuracy, completeness and consistency of the data over time. These criteria are the same as those used in the ISO 14064 certification process. The materiality assessment made it possible to exclude the calculation of the following categories: 2. Capital goods, 9. Downstream transport and distribution, 10. Processing of sold products, 12. End-life of sold products, 13. Leased assets, 14. Franchise. The total of Scope 3 emissions was 21,555.3 tCO₂, of which 94.3% is derived from primary data.

The reporting of CO₂ and Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions follows the GHG Protocol guidelines. Below are the methodologies, assumptions and emission factors used to calculate and measure emissions.

¹ In line with ESRS requirements, Scope 1 and 2 emissions are reported by including subsidiaries with a line-by-line method within the consolidation scope of the Juventus Consolidated Financial Statements. Scope 3 emissions are reported in accordance with materiality criteria and include emissions associated with the value chain of the Club's activities.

# E3-1 – POLICIES RELATED TO WATER AND MARINE RESOURCES

For Juventus, opportunities to reuse and streamline water resources, in order to achieve a positive impact, represent an important topic for its sports activities. The Club uses the aqueduct, the artificial pond at the JTCV the collection tank at JHQ as water withdrawal sources. Through the latter two, Juventus contributes to a more sustainable water supply, reusing rainwater and pursuing its commitment to reduce its water footprint, within a geographical area that is not water stressed to date, but which will be at high water risk in 2050, according to the projections of the Water Risk Atlas.

The topic of water resources, within the broader framework of environmental protection, is dealt with indirectly within the Environmental Policy, as described in section E1- "Climate change" (ref. E1-2 – "Policies related to climate change mitigation").

# E3-2 – ACTIONS AND RESOURCES RELATED TO WATER

Aware of the importance of water resources, the Company pays great attention to its management for the purpose of increasingly responsible consumption. Therefore, Juventus is committed to monitoring and reporting water consumption resulting from the pro-

cesses of its sports and business activities.

Juventus' water supply systems are based, as mentioned in the previous paragraph, mainly on water withdrawal from:

- municipal aqueducts;
- from the artificial pond of the JTCV, which serves as a collection basin and is used to irrigate the site's training pitches. There is currently no dedicated meter, but the Club is working to strengthen monitoring and improve data availability;
- from a water collection tank located at the JHQ.

Over the years, other Club facilities have also been equipped with rainwater collection systems. In particular, the Allianz Stadium and the JTCC have dedicated tanks, originally designed for pitch irrigating. However, technical evaluations have shown the presence of impurities in the collected water, which make its use both for irrigation and other purposes (e.g. toilets) complex and costly. A dedicated feasibility study confirmed that the available water would not be sufficient to justify the investment needed for the construction of treatment plants and new distribution networks.

# SECTION E3-4 – WATER CONSUMPTION SPECIFIES CONSUMPTION

Juventus has green areas covering a total of 128,000 m², used for sports activities, that are irrigated on average once a day in the winter season for sports needs and twice in the summer season, once for agronomic needs and the other for sports needs. In this context, in line with strategic ESG targets, irrigation methods and state-of-the-art technologies are used that make the use of water resources more efficient.

Another intervention area concerns the efficient management of irrigation of the Allianz Stadium pitch.

# THANKS TO THE IMPLEMENTATION OF SENSORS THAT MEASURE SOIL HUMIDITY IN REAL TIME, IT WAS POSSIBLE TO REDUCE THE IRRIGATION AND REDUCE WATER CONSUMPTION.

The plant is integrated with a weather station that daily records the grassland evaporation and transpiration rate, optimal water needs to be guaranteed without wa-

ste. In addition, the irrigation system is divided into single provision stations, which allow the irrigation of only the areas that actually need it, further reducing waste

The same efficiency logic was extended to training centres.

# IN THE LAST FOUR YEARS, ON FOUR PITCHES AT THE JTCV, A BERMUDA GRASS HAS BEEN INTRODUCED. THIS IS A WARM SEASON GRASS RESISTANT TO HIGH TEMPERATURES, WHICH HAS ALLOWED WATER SAVINGS OF 20% IN THE SUMMER MONTHS.

At the same time, a sensor system for monitoring soil humidity has been implemented both at Continassa and on two Vinovo pitches, allowing more focused irrigation management.

In addition, all plants on the various sites are now remotely controlled, with the possibility of deactivating programs in real time in the event of unforeseen precipitation, avoiding unnecessary waste of water.

The topic of resource use and circular economy was integrated into Juventus' sustainability strategy, in particular within the "Assist to Circularity" pillar. The double materiality assessment carried out by Juventus, whose methodological approach is described in the chapter "General Disclosures", made it possible to identify the IROs related to the topic of circularity. IROs related to the topic of resource use and circular economy are closely linked to Juventus' strategy and business model, with the target of reducing waste of both inflowing and outflowing resources and adopting increasingly effective circularity practices.

The two negative impacts that have been identified are of actual materiality. The first concerns the need to make suppliers' supply of raw materials more efficient and sustainable, while ensuring respect for human rights along the supply chain. The second concerns the medical waste management generated by associated activities, with the need to strengthen collection, treatment and disposal procedures with a view to greater environmental responsibility. To address and mitigate its first impact, the Club has adopted guidelines for responsible procurement, strengthening collabora-

tion with suppliers to improve procurement practices and ensure ethical and sustainable standards. For the second impact, the Club has embarked on an improvement path aimed at the adoption of advanced collection and disposal solutions, with a particular focus on recovery and enhancement practices, including low environmental impact treatment technologies and energy recovery.

Moreover, the opportunity to develop long-term solutions aimed at the reuse of materials contained in core activity products was intercepted, thus contributing to reducing environmental impact and promoting a circular economy model.

It should be noted that during the reporting period, no consultation activities were implemented with the affected communities with particular attention to circular economy topics.

# E5-1 – POLICIES RELATED TO RESOURCE USE AND CIRCULAR ECONOMY

For the Club, embracing the principles of the circular economy is not only a strategic choice, but also a responsibility to contribute to a more sustainable future. The adoption of practices that promote the circularity of materials, the reuse of resources and the reduction of waste is an essential opportunity to minimise the negative environmental impact of the materials and products used by Juventus during sports and business activities.

For these reasons, over the years the Club has adopted various policies with which it is committed to ensuring the protection of the environment with respect to the use of resources and the topic of circularity, in particular through increasingly responsible procurement practices. These are reported in section E1 – “Climate change” (ref. E1-2 – “Policies related to climate change mitigation”).

![img-89.jpeg](img-89.jpeg)

# E5-2 – ACTIONS AND RESOURCES RELATED TO RESOURCE USE AND CIRCULAR ECONOMY

In line with the “Assist to Circularity” pillar of the ESG strategy (see E5-3), Juventus is committed to monitoring and reporting the inflow and outflow of resources and materials used in the sport and business processes. In addition, the Club promotes initiatives to raise awareness on the topic, so that each person can make these principles their own and put them into practice in their daily lives.

Specifically, with regard to resource use and the circular economy, the following actions carried out during the 2024/2025 season are worth mentioning:

- waste management and monitoring: Please refer to section E5-5 of the document;
- match day and food & beverage: In the hospitality areas, the planning of food and drink orders is carefully calibrated with respect to the fan influx forecasts (based on the type of match, time and day of the match), with the target of reducing waste.

FOOD SURPLUSES ARE MANAGED BY THE EXTERNAL CATERER AND DONATED TO THE BANCO ALIMENTARE. ALSO WITH A VIEW TO CIRCULARITY, ALL HOSPITALITY AREAS AND THE STADIUM KIOSKS/BARS HAVE COMPLETED THE TRANSITION TO COMPOSTABLE OR RECYCLABLE PACKAGING, REPLACING SINGLE-USE PLASTIC;

- management of sports pitches: grass mowing cuttings resulting from maintenance of the playing pitches is sent to collection centres and used as biodegradable material for compost production.
- internal awareness-raising:

JUVENTUS TACKLES THE TOPIC OF THE TRANSITION TO A CIRCULAR ECONOMY THROUGH THE STRATEGIC “ASSIST TO CIRCULARITY” PILLAR.

The basis of this pillar is the 4R Approach, i.e. the application of the principles Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, and Recover principles in taking the Company’s activities forward. An aspiration of this type, for its implementation, cannot ignore the engagement of all people working in the Club. In fact, the “circularity” path includes the small acts of every person, repeated daily, that can make a huge difference, especially if considered from

a collective point of view. This includes the targeted energy consumption reduction and employee engagement through the AWorld platform, which provides training content, quizzes and the possibility of registering sustainable daily actions, including those related to circularity.

The management of the Club’s environmental events and processes is aligned with the international standards ISO 14001 (Environmental Management) and ISO 20121 (Sustainable Event Management), for which Juventus is certified.

In addition, following the results that will emerge from the LCA analysis referred to in paragraph E1-3 – Actions and resources in relation to climate change policies, the Club will assess specific intervention actions that may also include the progressive phasing out of virgin resources.

# E5-3 – TARGETS RELATED TO RESOURCE USE AND CIRCULAR ECONOMY

At present, Juventus is in the process of defining specific targets and actions (in line with the requirements of ESRS E5-3) aimed at circular economy. The use of resources is in fact one of the six pillars of the Black, White & More ESG Strategy: Assist to Circularity.

This pillar has the target to promote initiatives to support circularity through the reduction of resource consumption, the recovery and reuse of goods and materials distributed during events and at the Club’s venues.

In line with the ISO 14001 and ISO 20121 certified environmental management systems, Juventus also defines operational targets annually which include activities to streamline the use of resources and improve separate collection and recycling processes.

Although these commitments are not formalised as specific quantitative targets, they concretely contribute to the progress of the Club’s circular strategy. In a time horizon consistent with the definition of a broader Environmental Plan, the Club will define more structured and measurable targets relating to the use of resources and circular economy, in line with the requirements of ESRS E5, consistent with the “Assist to Circularity” pillar and with the commitments assumed by the Club within its certified environmental management systems.

In addition, materials and products used in green management are essential for sports activities. Organic and chemical fertilizers, pesticides, seeds and sand are essential elements for the effective and safe development and maintenance of green areas, to protect staff and players. At the same time, Juventus adopts management techniques aimed at ensuring the sustainable use of these materials, reducing the environmental impact of operations. These include the use of UVC disease control machines resulting in reduced plant protection treatments, the use of fans to lower humidity and reduce the risk of pathogens inoculation, the adoption of slow-release fertilisers to limit nitrate leaching in the soil and the use of permitted fertilisers and biostimulants in organic farming.

Match day and no-match-day material. The inflow of resources for the match-day event, which is the focus of business activities, includes all materials used to set up not only the playing pitch but also for the spaces in front of it such as changing rooms, VIP hospitality areas, conference rooms, stands and areas of access to the Stadium where bars and entertainment services are located. The flow of resources for these occasions focuses mainly on food, plastics for choreographies and set-ups, and cleaning service materials. In addition, some Stadium areas are also temporarily active outside the match-day (no-match-day) event. In addition to other events organised by Juventus, there is also the possibility of organising conferences, business meetings, corporate dinners, conventions or other tailored events made in the specific Stadium spaces.

In the case of choreographies established for the most significant home matches, materials certified according to the required safety requirements (e.g. fire-retardant certification) are used. Currently the selection mainly favours technical compliance criteria, while the Club is starting an internal comparison to assess the integration of additional sustainability parameters, such as the use of recycled materials.

For the management of events organised at Allianz Stadium and other facilities, Juventus give preference to the use of rented materials, such as scenic installations and audio-video supports. This choice makes it possible to reduce waste production and encourage the reuse of materials until the end of their useful life. In this way, installations do not entail disposable materials but can be reused several times, in line with the principles of circular economy.

With regard to the J Hotel, the most important resource inflows are food, beverages, elements for the restaurant such as glasses, plates, cutlery, tablecloths and containers (which have not been shown in the table due their weight estimate not being available), and for room preparation and cleaning (bed linen, towels, toilet paper, disinfectants, detergents).

# IN COMPLIANCE WITH ITS P ENVIRONMENTAL RESPONSIBILITY PRINCIPLES, THE COMPANY HAS GIVEN PREFERENCE TO OF CLEANING SERVICES PROVIDERS THAT USE SUSTAINABLE PROCESSES, MATERIALS AND PRODUCTS.

An example of this is SAMSIC Italia, cleaning service provider for all Juventus sites, with the following ESG certifications:

- ISO 9001, 14001, 45001;
- EU Ecolabel;
- LEED O+M Gold;
- UNI 11352;

- ISO 50001;
- ISO 30415 Diversity & Inclusion;
- ISO 14064 Carbon Footprint;
- UNI/PDR 125;
- SA8000;
- Ecovadis Gold;
- ISO 27001, 37001;
- 3-star Legality Rating;
- SOA OG1 - OG11;
- F-GAS.

The cleaning service at the Juventus sites is Ecolabel EU certified, a mark of environmental excellence that has been issued in light of the meeting of high environmental standards throughout the service life cycle. Criteria are met such as the periodic training of personnel on topics related to the use of products and the environmental impact of the service, the use of certified products with a low environmental impact, the separate collection of waste generated during the cleaning service, efficiency of energy and water consumption of the equipment and machinery used.

In particular, the adoption of ecological detergents, recyclable materials and solutions that comply with recognised environmental criteria is promoted. For example, products are formulated in compliance with the Ecolabel Regulations Resolution (EU) 2017/1217 and comply with the UNI EN ISO 14024 - Type 1 Environmental Product Labelling standard:

- for cleaning windows, glass, mirrors and other surfaces in offices and shared living spaces (DART ECO)
- degreasing detergent for routine cleaning of surfaces and equipment in kitchens, canteens (CHANTAL ECO)
- degreasing detergent for washing floors, walls and various surfaces (GRIT ECO)
- descaling detergent gel for bathrooms (SANDET ECO)
- descaling detergent for bathrooms ready for us (SANOCIT ECO and SANOCIT ECO 3).

# E5-5 – RESOURCE OUTFLOWS

The adoption of practices that promote the circularity of materials, the reuse of resources and the reduction of waste is an essential to minimise the environmental impact of the services offered by Juventus. The implementation of circular approaches is a key element in ensuring the Company's competitiveness in the sports industry, where market demand focused on the sustainability of products and services is constantly growing. For this reason, it is essential to manage outflows and waste generated according to circularity practices.

# RESOURCE OUTFLOWS

Juventus is committed to promoting solutions that promote the reuse of materials used in its activities, with particular regard to those used during events, laying the foundations for a continuous improvement path in the circular economy.

With regard to good circularity practices, at the end of the match-day event, leftover food from bars and restaurants is donated to the Banco Alimentare in Turin, with a significant reduction in waste.

# WASTE

Both in sports and business activities, Juventus is responsible for managing different types of waste, particularly during match day events. Operating in a service sector, and not in production, most of the resource inflows (please refer to section E5-4) are used during activities, subsequently turning into waste. This dynamic highlights the importance of effective waste management, especially at large turnout events.

The Company monitors its waste production and ensures its proper disposal through the ISO 14001 Environmental Management System. This procedure differentiates the management of hazardous from non-hazardous waste. All waste is falls under municipal waste and is consequently managed by local municipal authorities: this has defined the destination of the type of waste (there is currently no continuous measurement system for weight and type of waste: this aspect represents a potential area for improvement). Specifically, mixed waste is sent to a waste-to-energy plant¹⁰, while paper, glass and plastic are recycled. Organic waste is managed through aerobic and anaerobic digestion¹¹. Finally, hazardous waste is related to health/medical waste (mapped as a negative impact) and separate from that related to green maintenance. Hazardous waste produced by the sports area mainly consists of residues of contaminated health materials, such as needles, plasters, gauze and bandages. At the end of the matches, at the stadium, the medical staff collects these waste in eco-boxes that comply with current regulations. Each eco-box comes with a PVC bag in which the waste is placed and subsequently sealed. On the day following matches (match day+1), medical waste is weighed and placed in its dedicated temporary storage area. Within the time required by the regulations, the specialised company appointed by Juventus then ensures the collection, transport and disposal to authorised disposal plants. This procedure is applied in a systematic manner at the stadium and, with specific timelines for the activities carried out, also at other Club sites producing similar medical waste.

In parallel, the collaboration with the Sant'Anna School of Advanced Studies in Pisa has allowed sample analyses to be carried out on the product composition of waste, identifying areas with greater impact and possible corrective actions, such as the enhancement of containers and signage.

# SOCIAL INFORMATION (S1)

## S1 OWN WORKFORCE

In Juventus people represent the Club's growth and competitiveness driver. With skills, passion and team spirit, people contribute every day to management of challenges of an increasingly dynamic international context. Juventus strength lies in the ability to interpret the evolution of the sports industry and create value for fans, partners and communities, thanks to the harmonious work of those who operating with dedication in each area of the Club, on and off the pitch.

### SBM-2 – INTERESTS AND VIEWS OF STAKEHOLDERS

The people of Juventus represent a central element in the Club's strategic guidelines since their engagement, their well-being and their professional growth are considered decisive factors for the success of the organisation.

In particular, the Club deemed it essential to directly engage its own workforce during the materiality assessment (see chapter 'General Disclosures'), recognising the strategic value of employees' views and feedback to define sustainability priorities and identify the most material topics. This participation made it possible to gather valuable internal views, strengthening the link between business choices and the real needs of the internal community.

In addition to this specific engagement, throughout the year Juventus activates various business environment listening and monitoring tools – such as the survey sent to the all the employees on occasion of the World Mental Health Day – which allow to assess the satisfaction levels, identify areas for improvement and plan targeted actions. These initiatives allow for continuous and transparent dialogue, creating conditions for an increasingly inclusive and growth-oriented working environment.

### PEOPLE FIRST

**THE "PEOPLE FIRST" PILLAR OF THE "BLACK, WHITE & MORE" ESG STRATEGY EMPHASISES THE CENTRAL IMPORTANCE OF PEOPLE WITHIN THE COMPANY.**

In particular, it highlights Juventus' commitment to:

*'integrate ESG principles into the culture and activities of the Club, sports and not, to empower people, through:*

- *• virtuous paths of development, involvement and well-being;*
- *• a work environment that inspires excellence and a sense of belonging to a great team'.*

This pillar stems from the awareness - and belief - that sustainability is not an exclusive expense of a dedicated team, but a responsibility shared by each person within the organisation.

Each team, role, individual can generate an environmental and social impact. This means that the success of the deployment of the ESG Strategy depends not only on the actions of the dedicated team, but - above all - from the daily actions of each person at the Club, and their alignment with the strategy and values it embodies.

The double materiality exercise carried out by Juventus, whose methodological approach is described in section ESRS 2, made it possible to identify the main impacts on its employees, as well as the risks and opportunities associated with them. IROs related to the theme of own workforce are closely linked to Juventus' strategy and business model, with the target of creating a safe, inclusive, fair and focused work environment marked by the physical and mental well-being of employees, technical staff and players.

The main risks concern the mental and physical health of players and employees, with possible injuries impacting on performance and operational continuity, but also illicit or inappropriate behaviour - including those on social media - that can generate reputational damage, sanctions and loss of trust. In addition to this is the risk of not being able to attract and retain talent, with an increase in turnover and consequent negative effects on the Company's image and results. Conversely, opportunities arise from investments in professional well-being and growth, which improve satisfaction, productivity and retention, while Diversity, Equity & Inclusion policies strengthen attractiveness in the labour market and reputation.

# S1-1 - POLICIES RELATED TO OWN WORKFORCE

Over the years, the Club has adopted various policies aimed at ensuring an inclusive, safe and respectful work environment, in line with international best practices and current regulations¹⁹. These policies cover various aspects, including health and safety, quality of services in the medical sector, and diversity criteria.

By implementing them, Juventus is committed to creating a climate of trust and collaboration, valuing diversity and preventing any form of discrimination. In this context, the Club not only aims to meet the needs of its employees, but also seeks to build a solid and sustainable corporate culture, capable of facing future challenges with determination and responsibility. At the basis of all the Policies mentioned below is Code of Ethics (see the chapter "Governance Information") which establishes the principles and values that characterise the Undertaking's culture and guide the relationship with human resources.

# PEOPLE FIRST POLICY AND UNI PDR 125:2022 CERTIFICATION

Among the main topics promoted and disseminated by Juventus' corporate culture are diversity and inclusion, essential elements of regulations, procedures and policies which define the Company's actions not only in terms of corporate bodies, but of the corporate population as a whole. These values not only represent statements of principle, but form the basis for building a fair, respectful and open working environment open to each individual's contribution.

Confirming this commitment, the Club Code of Ethics clearly enshrines Juventus' position against all forms of discrimination, including social discrimination, racism, xenophobia and intolerance. Furthermore, the Club is committed to avoiding all forms of discrimination in its conduct and to respect differences in age, gender, sexual orientation and identity, ethnicity, religion, state of health, political and union membership, language or different abilities in relations with its stakeholders.

In April 2025,
